chunks: Abu al-Hasan (peace be upon him) said to me: 'O Muhammad! Are you more intense in taqlid, or the Murjiites?'
He said: I said, 'We are in taqlid and they are in taqlid.' So he said: 'I did not ask you about this.' So there was no answer with me beyond the first answer.

Then Abu al-Hasan (peace be upon him) said: 'Indeed, the Murjiites established a man whose obedience was not obligatory, and they followed him in taqlid. And you have established a man whose obedience is obligatory, and then you did not follow him in taqlid. Therefore they are more intense in taqlid than you.'

key_terms.المرجئة: Murjiites — an early Islamic theological sect who deferred judgment on major sins, holding that faith alone suffices regardless of deeds; they followed their own leadership structure
key_terms.تقليد: Taqlid — emulation or following a religious authority; in Shia theology this refers to following the Imam whose authority is divinely ordained
key_terms.طاعة: Obedience/ta'a — in this context, divinely-mandated obedience to the Imam, distinguishing Shia belief from the Murjiite model
key_terms.نصب: To establish/appoint — used for both the Murjiites appointing a leader and the Shia recognizing the Imam's position

ai.seo_question: What did Imam al-Ridha say about Shia taqlid compared to the Murjiites?
ai.summary: Imam Ali al-Ridha (AS) challenges his companion Muhammad ibn Ubayda with a pointed question about taqlid (emulation/following a religious authority). When Muhammad gives a vague answer equating both groups, the Imam clarifies the critical distinction: the Murjiites follow a leader whose obedience God has not made obligatory, while the Shia acknowledge the Imam's divinely-mandated authority but then fail to actually follow him. The Imam's argument is that true consistency demands following what one has already recognized as obligatory — the Shia's own creed obligates them to follow the Imam more rigorously than the Murjiites follow their self-chosen leader.
